label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, Judge **Carter refused to set aside 20,000 California ballots** on Wednesday, writing that it would 'wreak havoc' on an election already underway, and the DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit at once (CNN, NPR, Fox News, CalMatters). With five days left, CNN's average has Democrats up about 9 points on the generic ballot, and a Fox poll has Texas's Senate race tied at 49% (CNN, Fox News). On the economy, Q3 GDP grew 3.4% and September PCE inflation hit 3.6%, a day after the Fed held at 3.75% to 4% with two dissents for a hike; **futures see a December increase** (FXStreet, Axios, CNBC). Alphabet fell about 10% premarket on negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion while Microsoft rose about 4% on 48% Azure growth, and **Amazon reports after the close today** (CNBC, Bloomberg). Mediators led by Qatar are pressing Iran on enriched uranium while U.S. officials plan heavy strikes after Nov. 3, and Iran reportedly rejected the latest proposal (Axios, CNBC). In California, **Prop 40 now trails 46% to 52%** in the new PPIC poll, and SEIU Local 1000 and Newsom resume talks Friday (CalMatters, CBS San Francisco). Israel's count still leaves neither bloc at 61 seats (Axios, NPR, CNN). In tech, the Energy Department offered Constellation up to $5 billion to boost nuclear output, and **Anthropic's public S-1 shows $16.3 billion in first-half revenue** and founder voting control (TechCrunch, CNBC).

Judge Carter denied the DOJ's bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots and the DOJ appealed; a Ninth Circuit move could come before Nov. 3.
Prop 40 (billionaire tax) fell to 46% yes and 52% no in the latest PPIC poll, with the election on Tuesday.
State worker mediation resumes Friday, Oct. 30, after the first SEIU Local 1000 strike.

Alphabet drops about 10% premarket on negative free cash flow; Microsoft gains on 48% Azure growth.

markets.wrap: Stocks closed Wednesday slightly higher, with the S&P 500 up 0.28% to 7,743.98, the Dow up 0.19% and the Nasdaq up 0.27% (live data). Oracle rose about 11% after capping outside financing at $20 billion and projecting $225 billion in fiscal 2030 revenue (CNBC). **Thursday opens on a split in AI spending**: Alphabet was down about 10% premarket and Microsoft up nearly 4%, and Nasdaq-100 futures were down more than 1% (CNBC). WTI crude settled near $101 as renewed peace efforts eased supply fears (CNBC), and **Amazon reports after the close** (CNBC). Watchlist quotes below are Wednesday's closes, before the earnings reactions.

stories.title: Judge Carter refuses to set aside 20,000 California mail ballots, and the DOJ appeals
stories.summary: Carter denied the DOJ's restraining order Wednesday, saying it would 'wreak havoc' on an ongoing election; DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit.
story: U.S. District Judge David Carter on Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, denied the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order that would have made California set aside about 20,000 mail ballots tied to voters the federal government flagged as likely noncitizens. In a 26-page order, he wrote that the request "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway" and "violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections" (CNN, NPR, The Hill, Fox News, CalMatters). The DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit right away, and U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said the department would seek an emergency order (CNN).

The case reached Carter after he took it over from a Trump appointee. On Monday, a three-judge Ninth Circuit panel dismissed the DOJ's first emergency appeal 2-1, saying it had come before the trial judge ruled (The Hill, Fox News, CNN). At Tuesday's hearing Carter was openly skeptical and told DOJ lawyers to "Go out and indict," and some previews had said he might appoint a special master and push a final answer past Election Day. He did not do that; he ruled on the restraining order instead (Fox News, CalMatters).

Carter also noted that people the federal government recently labeled noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalized citizens (CNN). The DOJ and Homeland Security say their list identifies more than 20,000 registered Californians who are likely noncitizens and were sent ballots. California officials say processed ballots cannot be separated from the rest and that the underlying data produces false positives. CalMatters described the order as finding the request to be attempted election interference.
The practical effect is that California counties keep counting these ballots like any others, unless the Ninth Circuit or the Supreme Court steps in before or after Nov. 3.
stories.flag: Whether the Ninth Circuit will act on the new emergency appeal before Election Day has not been reported.
facts: Carter's order came Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, and ran 26 pages (CNN).
The DOJ list covers about 20,000 California mail ballots tied to suspected noncitizens.
A Ninth Circuit panel dismissed the DOJ's first appeal 2-1 on Monday as premature.
The DOJ appealed Carter's denial to the Ninth Circuit immediately.
No special master was appointed, despite pre-hearing reports that he might.
stories.left: Supporters of California's position argue that an election already in progress cannot be rewritten by a federal list with a documented error history. Naturalized citizens have been wrongly flagged in other states, so setting their ballots aside risks disenfranchising eligible voters days before the election. States, not Washington, run elections, and the remedy for any real noncitizen voting is prosecution after the fact, not holding back ballots in bulk.
stories.right: Conservatives argue the federal government has a duty to keep noncitizens from voting and that DHS and DOJ identified specific registrants. Asking for suspect ballots to be segregated, not destroyed, is a modest step that preserves the ability to verify citizenship before they are counted. Once commingled with other ballots they cannot be removed, so the argument is that a court should have acted before the count, not after.
stories.next: Watch for a Ninth Circuit ruling on the DOJ's emergency motion before Nov. 3, and whether the case reaches the Supreme Court.

stories.title: Democrats hold a steady lead in the final week as Trump campaigns in red states
stories.summary: CNN's average has Democrats up about 9 points on the generic ballot; Trump campaigned in Texas, where a Fox poll shows a tie.
story: With five days left before the Nov. 3 midterms, CNN's Poll of Polls, updated Oct. 27, shows Democrats ahead by about 9 points on the generic House ballot. Individual polls range from D+8 (NPR/PBS/Marist and CBS/YouGov) to D+11 (New York Times/Siena). CNN notes that neither party has won the House popular vote by 10 points or more in a midterm since 1986. Trump held rallies Tuesday in Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Texas, alongside Senate nominee Ken Paxton (CNN, Fox News).

A Fox News poll released Oct. 21 had Paxton and Democrat James Talarico tied at 49% in Texas, a state Trump won by double digits in 2024. Trump has spent much of the final stretch in other deep-red states, including Kentucky, Alabama, Nebraska, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Tennessee (CNN, The Hill). CNN's approval average puts him near 34%, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll cited by The Hill had it at 32% of U.S. adults.

Fox News's power rankings moved Ohio's Senate and governor's races to Lean Democratic in one recent update, and Republicans are defending seats in Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Kansas where polling is tight. CNN's analysis of how to tell whether Democrats are heading for a landslide points to the size of the House popular-vote margin and to results in districts Trump won.
Poll averages are not seat counts. House outcomes depend on district lines and turnout, and polls have missed in both directions before.
facts: CNN's generic-ballot average is about D+9 as of Oct. 27.
Fox News had Texas's Senate race tied at 49% on Oct. 21.
Trump's approval is about 34% in CNN's average and 32% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll (The Hill).
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
stories.left: Democrats read the numbers as a referendum on prices, the Iran war and Trump's red-state scramble. A president defending states he won by double digits is playing defense, they argue, and the generic-ballot lead is large and consistent across pollsters. The party's pitch is affordability, with inflation back above 3% and gas prices high.
stories.right: Republicans say midterm polls routinely overstate the out-party's strength and that Trump's rallies are aimed at turnout among low-propensity voters who respond to him and not to generic ballots. They point to competitive Senate races in Texas, Iowa and Ohio as proof the map is not lost, and argue that Democrats are running on opposition with no agenda on inflation or the border.
stories.next: Polls close Tuesday, Nov. 3; California's count will run for days afterward.

stories.title: Mediators press Tehran as the U.S. readies a week of strikes after the midterms
stories.summary: Qatar leads a uranium-deal push while U.S. and Israeli officials plan heavy strikes after Nov. 3; Iran reportedly rejected the newest proposal.
story: Arab and regional mediators are pressing Iran to accept nuclear concessions before the U.S. midterms, with Qatar leading and Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey backing, Axios reported Wednesday. U.S. and Israeli officials told Axios that planned post-election action would include about a week of massive strikes on Iranian leadership, energy, nuclear and infrastructure targets. CNBC, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that Washington told several Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the midterms. Oil rose on the report and later eased as renewed peace efforts calmed supply fears (CNBC).

The core gap, per Axios, is sequencing. The U.S. wants Iran to give up its enriched uranium stockpile. Iran wants the U.S. to lift its naval blockade and release frozen funds first. Qatar floated letting UN inspectors into bombed nuclear sites in exchange for some sanctions relief. CNBC reported Thursday that a senior Iranian official rejected the latest Qatari proposal as unacceptable. The last confirmed U.S. strikes were Sept. 1, according to CNBC.

The administration has said it would hold off until after Nov. 3, so the post-election timing is widely reported but not confirmed by officials. Trump has said a decision is close. WTI crude, is near $101 in the latest market data.

A Washington Examiner opinion piece argued Trump's window for a deal is closing. Democrats have been united against the war and have forced war-powers votes, tying it to gas prices and affordability (CNN).
stories.flag: Strike timing comes from anonymous officials via Axios and the Wall Street Journal. The White House has not announced a plan.
facts: Qatar leads the mediation, backed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey (Axios).
The U.S. wants Iran's enriched uranium stockpile surrendered; Iran wants the blockade lifted and funds released first.
Planned strikes would last about a week and hit leadership, energy, nuclear and infrastructure targets (Axios).
WTI crude is near $101 (live data).
The last confirmed U.S. strikes were Sept. 1 (CNBC).
stories.left: Democrats argue the war has cost families money through higher gas prices and has no stated strategy or end date. They say Congress never authorized open-ended fighting, that planning a major escalation for the day after an election shows politics is driving timing, and that Gulf allies' repeated requests for diplomacy deserve more weight than they get.
stories.right: Conservative voices say Iran has used every pause to stall, and that credible force is the only thing that moves Tehran. They argue that surrendering the enriched uranium stockpile is the minimum for any deal, that sanctions relief before that would reward delay, and that Trump's deadline strategy has repeatedly brought Iran back to the table.
stories.next: The Nov. 3 election is the reported trigger; watch for a Qatari or U.S. announcement before then and for oil prices.

stories.title: Prop 40 billionaire tax falls behind in a new PPIC poll days before the vote
stories.summary: The Public Policy Institute poll has 46% of likely voters for the one-time wealth tax and 52% against, a reversal from September.
story: California's billionaire tax, Proposition 40, now trails in the latest Public Policy Institute of California poll: 46% of 1,086 likely voters support it and 52% oppose it, a reversal from September, when supporters held a slim 52% majority (CalMatters). Another poll from the Citrin Center and Politico had it at 46% yes and 43% no (CalMatters). Prop 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' net worth (Fox Business). Election Day is Nov. 3.

Money is lopsided. CalMatters reported that opponents had raised more than $205 million by mid-October, with Sergey Brin giving at least $102 million; the SF Chronicle counted a smaller figure for Brin and a larger total for the campaign, so estimates vary with timing. The campaign backing the tax, led by SEIU-UHW, has said it cannot match the opposition's TV spending and is relying on volunteers (SF Chronicle). Gov. Newsom opposes the measure.

Two companion measures, Props 41 and 42, are designed to nullify Prop 40 if both pass. In the earlier PPIC survey, Prop 41 led 51% to 44% and Prop 42 led 54% to 43%; I did not find their numbers in the newest poll. The state's Legislative Analyst said some billionaires may leave but estimated the behavioral effect at less than $1 billion a year (Fox Business).
stories.flag: Newest PPIC numbers for Props 41 and 42 were not found; the figures cited are from the earlier survey. Total opposition fundraising varies between $205 million and over $300 million depending on outlet and date.
facts: PPIC: 46% yes, 52% no among 1,086 likely voters (CalMatters).
Supporters led 52% in September.
Prop 40 is a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' net worth (Fox Business).
Opponents had raised more than $205 million by mid-October (CalMatters).
Props 41 and 42 would nullify Prop 40 if both pass.
stories.left: Supporters say the state faces health-care and services cuts and that a handful of billionaires have captured enormous gains while ordinary Californians pay for the budget. They argue a one-time tax is a modest ask, that threats to leave are bargaining tactics, and that the opposition's massive spending shows how much the measure would matter.
stories.right: Opponents say a net-worth tax is unprecedented, hard to value and administer, and would push founders and investors out, shrinking the income-tax base the state already depends on. They note that Newsom and prominent Democrats oppose it and that the Legislative Analyst warned of departures. Economists like Art Laffer called it a path to a California exodus (Fox Business).
stories.next: Election Day is Nov. 3; the Prop 41 and 42 results decide whether Prop 40 survives if it passes.

stories.title: California state workers and Newsom resume mediation Friday after the first-ever SEIU strike
stories.summary: SEIU Local 1000's one-day Oct. 21 strike is over, and talks restart Oct. 30 with pay, health costs and the four-day office mandate unresolved.
story: About 100,000 state workers belong to SEIU Local 1000, which staged its first strike in 44 years on Oct. 21. Tens of thousands walked off the job in Sacramento, San Francisco, Los Angeles and elsewhere, with DMV offices and parks limited (CalMatters, CBS San Francisco). A state-appointed mediator has scheduled the parties to resume talks on Oct. 30, a Friday, according to CalMatters. I found no report of a deal.

The union wants a 20% raise over three years, more state money toward health care, and clear telework rules, CBS reported. Its contract expired June 30. Newsom's order requiring most employees in the office four days a week took effect in July, and he vetoed AB 1729, which would have let departments set their own telework policies. In late September the Public Employment Relations Board found CalHR had not met and conferred in good faith (CalMatters). About 5,000 workers deemed essential did not strike.

CalHR says it is open to negotiating and wants a fair and responsible agreement. In 2025, Local 1000 and most other unions accepted two years of wage reductions in exchange for days off, which union members now cite as part of their anger (CalMatters).
Newsom leaves office in January, which gives both sides a deadline of sorts.
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by center and left-leaning outlets; no right-leaning coverage of this strike found.
facts: SEIU Local 1000 represents about 100,000 state workers.
The Oct. 21 strike was the union's first in 44 years.
92.6% of voting members authorized a strike (CBS).
Mediation resumes Oct. 30.
Newsom vetoed AB 1729, which would have loosened telework rules.
stories.left: Labor advocates say state workers took pay cuts last year, face a health-care cost squeeze and are being forced back to the office for a mandate Newsom would not soften even when the Legislature passed a bill. They add that a labor board found the state bargained in bad faith, and that a 44-year first strike shows how far the relationship has fallen.
stories.right: Fiscal conservatives would say the state is facing budget pressure and that public-sector raises compete with services taxpayers fund. They would also argue that in-office work for state employees is a reasonable expectation, since the public pays for those jobs.
stories.next: Mediation resumes Friday, Oct. 30; a second strike has not been announced.

stories.title: A one-city ceasefire holds in Oleshky as Putin agrees in principle to resume talks
stories.summary: A pause in fighting brokered with Melania Trump's involvement took effect Tuesday, while the wider war and peace talks remain unsettled.
story: A localized ceasefire took effect early Tuesday in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's Kherson region, so aid can enter and civilians can be evacuated. The White House said Melania Trump secured it, and officials said it held through its first 30 hours (NPR, NBC News). Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it stopped firing in the Kherson direction, and the Kremlin spokesman credited her and said it was discussed in a recent Putin-Trump call (NBC News).

Up to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, and the U.N. says mines and drone attacks keep them from leaving (NBC News). Her adviser Marc Beckman told Fox News that she personally brokered the deal and that Russia agreed to extend it by two days and widen it; that claim has no independent confirmation. The Vatican said it was not aware of her role, and noted Pope Leo XIV called Putin about Oleshky on Oct. 16.

On the wider war, Putin told envoy Steve Witkoff last week that he is ready to resume direct talks, and Russia released a U.S. detainee (Axios). NPR reported Russia agreed to a trilateral meeting with U.S. and Ukrainian officials next month. Russia hit Kyiv with missiles and drones hours after agreeing to talks (NBC News, CNN). Zelensky has said he is open to freezing front lines to end the war (Fox News).
Moscow demands territory, including areas it does not fully control, and Kyiv rejects ceding sovereign land and wants enforceable security guarantees.
stories.flag: The claim that the truce was extended and widened comes from Melania Trump's adviser alone.
facts: The Oleshky ceasefire began early Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Up to 2,000 civilians remain in the town.
Putin said he is ready to resume direct talks with the U.S. (Axios).
Russia struck Kyiv after agreeing to talks.
Zelensky says he is open to freezing front lines.
stories.left: Critics argue Ukraine is being squeezed: Patriot deliveries have been delayed and Kyiv says Washington withheld early-warning data, which the U.S. denies. A first lady's local truce is welcome humanitarian news, they say, but it does not substitute for sustained military aid and pressure on Moscow, whose strikes continue during talks.
stories.right: Supporters of the administration say direct engagement with Putin is producing results the previous approach did not: a detainee release, a local ceasefire and a path to trilateral talks. They argue that a freeze along current lines may be the realistic way to stop the killing and that European partners should carry more of the cost.
stories.next: A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting is expected next month; watch for a date and venue.

stories.title: Israel's count still shows neither bloc at 61 seats as coalition talks loom
stories.summary: With most votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc has 53 to 54 seats, the opposition 47 to 48, and Arab parties hold a record 19.
story: With about 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc was projected at 53 seats, down from 68 in the outgoing Knesset, and Eisenkot's opposition bloc at 48, according to NPR and Axios. A later CNN update put the blocs at 54 and 47. Netanyahu's party leads with a projected 26 seats and Eisenkot's Yashar has 21. The Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List are projected at a combined 19, a record. Turnout was about 77.7%, the highest since 1999 (CNN, Axios).

About 500,000 votes remain, from soldiers, diplomats and prisoners, and Axios reported they are unlikely to change the balance. To reach 61, the opposition would need Arab-party support. Netanyahu has ruled out working with them, while Eisenkot has shown some openness (Axios). Netanyahu claimed victory and alleged serious criminal activity during voting in Arab areas (Fox News, CNN).

President Isaac Herzog will consult the parties and choose the candidate most likely to assemble a 61-seat majority, not necessarily the leader of the largest party. If that fails, lawmakers get 21 days to back another candidate (Axios, CNN).
Expect weeks of bargaining and possibly another election.
stories.flag: Seat totals are projections, and sources differ by one or two seats.
facts: Netanyahu's bloc: 53-54 seats projected, down from 68.
Opposition bloc: 47-48 seats.
Arab parties: a record 19 combined.
Turnout: about 77.7%, highest since 1999.
Herzog picks who tries to form a government.
stories.left: Center-left commentators read the result as a rebuke of Netanyahu, whose bloc lost 14 or 15 seats, and say any government should reflect that. They argue Arab citizens' record turnout makes their representatives legitimate partners, and that calling their votes criminal without evidence undermines the vote.
stories.right: Netanyahu's supporters argue his party is still the largest and that his bloc remains well ahead of any rival alliance without Arab parties. They say governing with parties that oppose Israel's character as a Jewish state would be unstable, and that claims of irregularities in some areas deserve investigation.
stories.next: Official results are expected by Nov. 4, followed by Herzog's consultations.

stories.title: Q3 growth beats forecasts at 3.4% while September inflation runs hotter, after the Fed holds with two hike dissents
stories.summary: GDP grew 3.4% annualized, September PCE inflation hit 3.6%, and traders see a December hike after Wednesday's split Fed decision.
story: The Commerce Department's advance estimate shows U.S. GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second and above the roughly 3.2% economists expected (FXStreet, Quartz, CNBC). The September PCE price index rose 0.5% for the month, taking the annual rate to 3.6%, while core PCE rose 0.3% to 3.1%, in line with forecasts (FXStreet). Axios reported that annual inflation rose from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.

On Wednesday the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point hike, Axios and the Washington Examiner reported. It was Cook's first dissent since she joined the Fed in 2022, and she faces a White House hearing on her possible removal over alleged mortgage fraud, which her lawyers call a pretext (Axios). CME's FedWatch showed about an 85% chance of a December hike, per Axios.

Chair Kevin Warsh said growth has firmed and that committee members have "no tolerance" for persistently elevated inflation, a line Fox Business had quoted earlier. He also announced that one 2027 meeting will focus on strategy, with no rate vote or policy statement (CNBC, Axios).
The mix of strong growth and hot prices is what pushes officials toward tightening. Advance GDP estimates are revised, so the 3.4% figure can still move.
facts: Advance Q3 GDP: 3.4% annualized, versus about 3.2% expected.
September PCE: +0.5% on the month, 3.6% on the year; core 3.1%.
The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28.
Cook and Hammack dissented for a quarter-point hike.
Futures show roughly an 85% chance of a December hike (CME via Axios).
stories.left: Progressives worry that hiking into an energy-price shock caused partly by a war would hit workers and borrowers hardest, and that the Fed is risking a downturn to fight inflation it did not cause. They also see the effort to remove Cook, an independent governor, as a threat to the central bank's independence.
stories.right: Conservative economists argue inflation above 3% for years justifies the hawks, and that the Fed was slow to tighten. They say energy-price shocks become entrenched if policy waits, and that two dissents for a hike show the committee's center is moving. Some also note the political pressure Trump has put on the Fed to cut.
stories.next: September PCE data landed today; the Fed meets again in mid-December, and futures lean toward a hike.

stories.title: Alphabet heads for its worst post-earnings drop while Microsoft rises on Azure
stories.summary: Alphabet fell about 10% premarket on negative free cash flow and an EPS miss; Microsoft gained about 4% after Azure grew 48%.
story: Alphabet shares were down about 10% in premarket trading Thursday, putting the stock on course for its biggest post-earnings drop ever, CNBC reported. The company posted third-quarter free cash flow of negative $9.07 billion against a consensus of negative $2.70 billion. CNBC attributed part of that to a $5.2 billion payment tied to a European Commission fine and a build-up of inventory for TPU system sales. Adjusted EPS fell 7% to $2.67 versus $3.02 expected, and Bloomberg said search ad sales missed forecasts.

Google Cloud was the bright spot, with revenue roughly doubling to $30.71 billion (CNBC). Alphabet kept its 2026 capital spending guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion and said it expects a significant increase in 2027 (CNBC). Nasdaq-100 futures were down more than 1% early Thursday.

Microsoft rose nearly 4% premarket. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.2 billion, and capital spending of $45.2 billion including finance leases came in below analyst projections. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but stayed positive (CNBC).
Amazon reports after the close today, and the bar is set by AWS's 37% growth in the second quarter (CNBC). Apple reports Nov. 2.
facts: Alphabet premarket: down about 10% (CNBC).
Q3 free cash flow: negative $9.07 billion versus negative $2.70 billion expected.
Adjusted EPS: $2.67 versus $3.02 expected.
Microsoft Azure: up 48% to $33.2 billion; stock up nearly 4% premarket.
Amazon reports after the close today; Apple on Nov. 2.
stories.why: Investors rewarded the company whose AI spending showed up as cloud revenue and punished the one whose cash drain widened. The split shows markets sorting AI spenders by return, not by size. Alphabet's 2027 capex warning keeps pressure on its cash.
stories.next: Amazon's report after the close today, then Apple on Nov. 2 and Nvidia on Nov. 18.

stories.title: Energy Department offers Constellation up to $5 billion to boost output at existing reactors
stories.summary: The conditional loan would fund upgrades adding about 1.1 gigawatts in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania, with tech firms buying most of the power.
story: The Energy Department offered Constellation a conditional loan of up to $5 billion to upgrade eight nuclear plants in Illinois, Maryland and Pennsylvania, adding about 1.1 gigawatts of capacity, Bloomberg and TechCrunch reported this week. The loan has not been finalized. Constellation says it plans to uprate 11 reactors, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright described 15 reactors at eight sites, so the counts differ by source. Most or all of the added power from seven of the facilities is already contracted to Google, Meta or Amazon (TechCrunch).

Uprating means getting more output from an existing reactor, often with equipment upgrades and sometimes more highly enriched fuel. MIT Technology Review framed the question as how much more existing plants can give. The department earlier this month lent Vistra $4.2 billion for upgrades at three plants, and previously gave Constellation $1 billion for the restart of Crane, the former Three Mile Island Unit 1 (CNBC, TechCrunch).

The pattern is federal credit supporting upgrades whose output data-center operators buy up front. It is faster than building new reactors, but each uprate needs regulatory review and gains are limited to the margin the original design allows.
stories.flag: Reactor counts differ: Constellation says 11, Wright said 15 at eight locations.
facts: Loan size: up to $5 billion, conditional and not final.
Capacity added: about 1.1 GW across eight plants in IL, MD and PA.
Seven facilities' added output is largely sold to Google, Meta or Amazon (TechCrunch).
Vistra received a $4.2 billion DOE loan earlier this month.
Constellation's Crane restart got a $1 billion loan last November.
stories.why: Uprates are the quickest way to add firm carbon-free power for AI data centers, because they reuse sites, grid connections and licenses. The loan shows the government underwriting the bet, and the contracts show tech buyers paying for it.
stories.next: Watch for a finalized loan agreement and Nuclear Regulatory Commission approvals for each uprate.

stories.title: SpaceX preps Starship Flight 15 and plans to try catching both stages
stories.summary: Booster 22 completed a static fire Oct. 25, and Musk says he expects a double catch in November.
story: SpaceX fired all of Super Heavy Booster 22's Raptor 3 engines for about 15 seconds on Oct. 25, the first major test before Starship Flight 15, Space.com reported. The booster will later be mated with Ship 42, which still has its own static fire and systems checks ahead. No official launch date has been announced, and Space.com said that if recent campaigns are a guide, liftoff could come in mid to late November.

On SpaceX's Q3 earnings call, Musk said the company will try to recover both the booster and the ship on Flight 15, calling it "more likely than not" to succeed (Space.com). Space.com noted that a ship catch is harder than a booster catch because the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster.

Flight 14 on Sept. 28 was the first Starship flight to reach orbit. The ship deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites over about 30 minutes and splashed down intact in the Pacific (Space.com). SpaceX also hopes to launch Starship from Florida for the first time before the end of the year.
A catch of both stages would be a step toward quick reuse, which Starship's cost model depends on.
stories.flag: Launch timing is Musk's estimate, not an FAA-licensed date; SpaceX has not confirmed a payload.
facts: Booster 22 static fire: Oct. 25, about 15 seconds, all Raptor 3 engines.
Flight 15 is expected in November, per Musk.
Musk said a double catch is more likely than not to succeed.
Flight 14 reached orbit and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.
Ship 42 still has tests to complete.
stories.why: Rapid reuse of both stages is what could cut launch costs sharply, and an orbital Starship that returns intact makes large Starlink deployments and lunar landers more plausible. A ship catch has never been tried.
stories.next: Ship 42's static fire, then an FAA license and launch date for Flight 15, likely in November.

stories.title: Lab model shows the embryo and uterine lining reshape each other at implantation
stories.summary: A Nature Cell Biology study found an endometrium-induced cell state in the embryo and flagged CSF3 signaling as a candidate regulator.
story: Researchers co-cultured human endometrial assembloids, lab-grown models of the uterine lining, with human blastocysts and blastoids, which are stem-cell-derived embryo models. A Nature Cell Biology paper by Bi, Tu, Wang and colleagues, published Oct. 27, reports that the endometrium induces a distinct trophoblast cell state in the embryo and that CSF3-CSF3R signaling is a candidate regulator of early implantation. A News & Views piece in the same journal, titled "Implantation begins with a conversation," frames the finding as a two-way exchange (Nature).

Implantation is a major point of failure in early pregnancy and is hard to study because it happens inside the body. Earlier assembloid work, including a 2024 Science Advances model built from gland-like organoids, stromal cells and an endothelial network, reproduced early implantation steps with blastoids and human blastocysts (Science Advances).

The new paper points to a specific signaling pathway to test. A candidate regulator in a dish is not yet proof that the same pathway drives implantation in a person, and the model leaves out immune and blood-vessel complexity of the real uterus.
If validated, the pathway could help explain some implantation failures.
facts: The paper was published in Nature Cell Biology on Oct. 27.
It used human endometrial assembloids with blastocysts and blastoids.
It found an endometrium-induced trophoblast cell state.
CSF3-CSF3R signaling is named as a candidate regulator.
The work is a lab model, not a clinical trial.
stories.why: Implantation failure is a leading barrier in fertility treatment, and models that capture the embryo-uterus dialogue let researchers test hypotheses without human subjects. The candidate pathway gives a concrete target for follow-up.
stories.next: Look for replication of the CSF3-CSF3R result and tests in more complex models.

stories.title: Monkey brains flicker about 15 times a second between what they see and what they miss
stories.summary: A UC Berkeley preprint found alternating neural patterns for a perceived and an unperceived image, suggesting timing matters for awareness.
story: A preprint from Doris Tsao's lab at UC Berkeley, posted on bioRxiv and not yet peer reviewed, reports that macaques' brain activity alternated about 15 times per second between a pattern for the image they consciously saw and a pattern for an image they did not perceive (Nature, Science). The team used flash suppression, with monkeys viewing a different image in each eye, and could reconstruct both the seen and the unseen images from neural activity alone with high fidelity.

The unperceived signal was strong, not faint as earlier monkey studies had suggested. Science's report says the findings hint that conscious perception may depend on when neural patterns appear, not only on which neurons are active (Science).

Outside researchers caution that this is far from settling the neural basis of consciousness. Shay Ben-Haim, who was not involved, told Science he wants to know whether the flicker appears in other brain regions and whether altering it changes perception.
Results from a preprint can change in review.
facts: The preprint comes from Doris Tsao's lab at UC Berkeley.
Brain activity alternated at about 15 Hz.
Both seen and unseen images could be reconstructed from neural data.
Outside researchers want tests in other brain regions.
Subjects were macaques, not humans.
stories.why: If awareness depends on timing, theories that focus on a single brain region or a threshold of activity may need revision. The method also gives researchers a way to read out what the brain holds but does not report.
stories.next: Watch for peer review and replication, and for causal tests that alter the flicker.

stories.title: Anthropic's public S-1 shows $16.3 billion in first-half revenue and unusual control rights
stories.summary: The filing, planned for Nasdaq under ANT, shows a small operating loss, a huge non-cash net loss and founder voting control.
story: Anthropic publicly filed its S-1 on Oct. 26 for a Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading, TechCrunch and CNBC reported. The filing shows revenue of nearly $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 and an operating loss of $693 million, down from $2.1 billion in the first half of 2025. Net loss was $80.7 billion, including a $72.4 billion non-cash charge tied to convertible debt accounting (CNBC). Anthropic did not disclose offering terms, and its run-rate revenue field is blank.

Reported valuation talk ranges from about $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, up from $965 billion in a May funding round (CNBC, Reuters via IPO Scoop). IPO Scoop, citing Bloomberg, said marketing could begin around the week of Nov. 9, though no roadshow date is confirmed.

Governance is the main issue for investors. A Long-Term Benefit Trust elects and can remove a majority of the board through a special Class T stock. Seven co-founders, including Dario Amodei, hold a single Class F share with 50.1% of the vote, so public holders would have little say (CNBC). CNBC also noted a sharp slowdown in revenue growth from the second to the third quarter and quoted investors split between calling the IPO a "generational moment" and "speculative fiction."
As a public benefit corporation, the company must balance public benefit with shareholder duties, which analysts say could affect valuation and takeover prospects (CNBC).
stories.flag: Valuation range and roadshow timing are reported, not set by the company; the S-1 does not state a price.
facts: Public S-1 filed Oct. 26; ticker ANT on Nasdaq.
First-half 2026 revenue was nearly $16.3 billion (CNBC).
Operating loss $693 million; net loss $80.7 billion, mostly non-cash.
Seven co-founders hold 50.1% of voting power through one Class F share.
Offering terms and price have not been disclosed.
stories.why: This is the first test of public markets' appetite for a frontier AI lab at trillion-dollar scale. The numbers show large revenue and an operating loss that is shrinking, while the control structure and growth slowdown are what investors are arguing about.
stories.next: Watch for the price range and roadshow start, possibly the week of Nov. 9.

stories.title: Data-center electricity costs became a midterm fight after a Senate bill stalled
stories.summary: The House passed a ratepayer bill 417-3, but Senate Democrats blocked it 57-43, and both parties now court voters angry about AI power demand.
story: The House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3 in September. It would require states to consider rules making large data centers cover new power costs, but it would not force them to adopt any (The Hill, Axios). In the Senate, a procedural vote to advance it failed 57-43, short of the 60 needed. Four Democrats voted with Republicans: Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock (The Hill). Sponsor Jon Husted of Ohio faces Democrat Sherrod Brown in a close Senate race.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the bill optional and a fraud, saying it requires no protections, and Democrats prefer a bill from Sen. Martin Heinrich that would make large users pay for grid upgrades (The Hill). The Washington Examiner framed the vote as Democrats denying Republicans a midterm win, and Fox News called it a midterm political play. The bill codifies Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

The politics are why. Axios reported in August that a GOP memo warned AI companies that data centers are "politically radioactive." Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro ordered developers to cover electricity costs and win local approval, and Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers called for a one-year state moratorium (The Hill).

Congress has not passed a federal AI framework. Trump's December executive order directs the Justice Department to challenge state AI laws, and the White House has asked Congress to preempt them (The Hill).
facts: The House passed the bill 417-3.
The Senate procedural vote failed 57-43; 60 were needed.
Four Democrats voted yes: Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock.
The bill would only require states to consider cost-allocation rules.
No federal AI framework has passed Congress.
stories.left: Democrats say the bill is a placebo that lets Republicans claim credit while requiring nothing, and that real protection means binding rules making the largest users pay for grid upgrades. They also warn that federal preemption of state AI laws would strip states of the only protections currently in force.
stories.right: Republicans say the bill is a bipartisan first step that passed the House 417-3, and that Senate Democrats killed it to deny Husted a win. They argue a national standard is better than a patchwork of state rules, and that tech companies should not get state-level fights over each project.
stories.why: AI's growth depends on power, and the political cost of that demand is landing on household bills. Rules on who pays will shape where data centers are built and how fast.
stories.next: Watch for a second attempt through permitting reform and for the Husted-Brown result on Nov. 3.

stories.title: Duchenne gene-editing trial that killed a boy in China showed limited benefit
stories.summary: Results of HuidaGene's base-editing trial say four children were treated, one died of an immune reaction, and editing effects were limited.
story: Results from the first human trial of a base-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy were published this week, and they are sobering. The trial, run by Shanghai company HuidaGene, treated four children using an adeno-associated virus to deliver a base editor to muscle. The therapy edited some target genes but produced limited benefit and caused a catastrophic immune reaction in one participant, a boy who died, Nature reported.

Science separately reported that another Shanghai-based biotech disclosed the death of a child in a Duchenne gene-editing trial a year earlier, following another gene-editing death in China that went undisclosed for 16 months. It is unclear from the reporting I found whether that case involves the same company.

Gene therapy for Duchenne has had safety problems elsewhere. Sarepta's Elevidys, which uses a different approach, was linked to two deaths from acute liver failure in non-ambulatory patients in 2025, according to a review article.
I found no reports of an FDA response or a regulatory hold tied to this trial.
stories.flag: It is unclear whether Science's second reported death involves the same HuidaGene program.
facts: The trial treated four children.
One boy died after an immune reaction.
Editing worked on some targets but benefit was limited.
The delivery method was an AAV carrying a base editor.
Science reported another undisclosed gene-editing death in China.
stories.why: High-dose viral delivery of gene editors can trigger severe immune reactions, and the trial's limited efficacy suggests the risk was not offset by benefit. Late disclosure of deaths also weakens oversight.
stories.next: Watch for regulator responses in China and for how other Duchenne editing programs adjust dosing and monitoring.

briefs: Oracle's stock rose about 11% Wednesday after it projected $225 billion in fiscal 2030 revenue and capped fundraising for fiscal 2027 through 2030 at $20 billion, split between equity and debt (CNBC).
Oracle said Tuesday it will integrate ChatGPT and Codex into its apps and offer Google's TPUs and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip on its cloud (CNBC).
Nvidia and AMD said they will invest a combined $4 billion in Meta's equity raise, Nvidia $3 billion and AMD $1 billion, as Meta plans to raise $95 billion for AI infrastructure (CNBC).
Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, a free open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages (TechCrunch).
Apple announced its first touchscreen Mac, a MacBook Pro with M5 Pro or Max chips, on sale Nov. 6 (CNBC).
